extracted.intended_audience: Catholic faithful and catechism students preparing for Mass, Communion, and sacramental practice
extracted.subtask_description: A catechetical set of rules, definitions, and behavioral requirements about indulgences, the Holy Eucharist, reception of Communion, the Mass as sacrifice, and proper conduct during and after Mass. Includes doctrinal definitions, liturgical procedure, and practical obligations for the faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indulgence: general requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain an indulgence we must be in a state of grace and perform the works enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For plenary indulgences additional acts are required (see separate criterion). 'Works' include visiting certain churches or altars, giving alms, saying certain prayers, etc. The requirement to be in a state of grace is foundational; the work enjoined must actually be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenary indulgence: additional requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plenary indulgence it is required, in addition to being in a state of grace and performing the works enjoined, to go to confession and Holy Communion, and to pray for the intention of our Holy Father the Pope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praying for the Pope's intention means praying for whatever he is praying for or wishes you to pray for (not necessarily for the Pope personally). For the papal intention it is sufficient to recite one Our Father and one Hail Mary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial indulgence: three basic ways
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial indulgence can be gained by: (1) raising one's heart to God amidst the duties and trials of life and making a pious invocation (even mentally); (2) giving of oneself or one's goods to those in need; (3) voluntarily depriving oneself of something pleasing in a spirit of penance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial indulgences are also granted for reciting certain well-known prayers (acts of faith, hope, charity, contrition) and for performing acts of devotion (e.g., making a Spiritual Communion). Using blessed devotional articles devoutly (Sign of the Cross, crucifix, scapular) may carry a partial indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention to gain indulgences
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain an indulgence you must have the intention of gaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many indulgenced prayers/acts are unknown to people, one may make a general intention each morning to gain all indulgences possible during the day, whether known or not; with that general intention, performing an indulgenced work gains the indulgence even if one did not know it applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of indulgence durations (e.g., '40 days')
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial indulgences were formerly designated by amounts of time (forty days, one hundred days, a year) which indicated the remission of temporal punishment equivalent to that early public penance would have required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numbers do not mean time off Purgatory; they recall how much temporal punishment the Church remitted compared to early Christians' public penances. The precise amount of temporal punishment corresponding to e.g. forty days is not known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Holy Eucharist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Holy Eucharist is the Sacrament which contains the body and blood, soul and divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ under the appearances of bread and wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When saying 'contains' the meaning is that the Sacrament is the body and blood itself—in a new form under appearances of bread and wine. 'Eucharist' means 'thanks' because Our Lord gave thanks before changing the bread and wine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution of the Eucharist
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ instituted the Holy Eucharist at the Last Supper the night before He died, in the presence of the twelve Apostles, by taking bread and wine, blessing, breaking, and giving it, saying 'This is My body' and 'This is My blood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words 'Do this for a commemoration of Me' establish the ongoing celebration of the Eucharist. The institution at the Last Supper and the exact words are the scriptural basis for the sacrament and for the priest's role in perpetuating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transubstantiation (change of substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Our Lord said 'This is My body' and 'This is My blood' the substance of the bread and wine was changed into the substance of His body and blood; the appearances (color, taste, figure, smell) remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Substance’ refers to what stands underneath sensible appearances; in the Eucharist only the substance is changed miraculously, while appearances remain unchanged. The reality of the change is known by Christ's words and by faith, not by the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real presence tied to appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Holy Eucharist is the body of Our Lord just as long as the appearances of bread and wine remain; when the appearances cease, Our Lord's bodily presence goes as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: after receiving Communion the appearance remains for about fifteen or twenty minutes; the faithful should remain and make thanksgiving during that time, bow their heads, speak to Our Lord, and avoid rushing out or immediate distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of Communion: essential requirements (good Communion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a good Communion it is necessary to be in a state of sanctifying grace, to be fasting for one hour, and to have a right intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'right intention' is a holy/spiritual motive (to obey Christ's command, to obtain strength to resist temptation, to be united with Our Lord). Water and true medicine do not break the fast and may be taken; if one accidentally breaks the fast, one should not go to Communion at that Mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fasting rule for Holy Communion and exceptions (Viaticum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fast necessary for Holy Communion is abstaining for one hour from everything taken as food or drink; anyone in danger of death is allowed to receive when not fasting (Viaticum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not fasting because of danger of death, the Communion is called Viaticum and the priest uses different prayers. The priest is obliged under pain of sin to bring Holy Communion to the dying at any hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of receiving in mortal sin
rubrics_metrics.description: He who receives Communion in mortal sin receives the body and blood of Christ, but does not receive His grace, and he commits a great sacrilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving into a soul burdened with mortal sin is compared to receiving a highly esteemed guest into an unclean house; it is both a loss of intended benefit and a grave offense deserving punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving plentifully the graces of Communion
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive plentifully the graces of Holy Communion it is not enough to be free from mortal sin; one should be free from all affection to venial sin and should make acts of lively faith, firm hope and ardent love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiritual dispositions beyond bare absence of mortal sin increase the fruitfulness of Communion; internal preparation and acts of devotion are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to receive Communion (when bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to receive Holy Communion, under pain of mortal sin, during the Easter time and when in danger of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The faithful should observe this liturgical obligation; exceptional circumstances (danger of death) also create duty to receive (and obligation of priest to bring Viaticum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of Communion (commendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well to receive Holy Communion often, as nothing is a greater aid to a holy life than often to receive the Author of all graces and the Source of all good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent reception is encouraged, within the requirements of state of grace and appropriate disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior after Communion and recommended thanksgiving
rubrics_metrics.description: After Holy Communion we should spend some time in adoring Our Lord, in thanking Him for the graces we have received and in asking Him for the blessings we need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, remain about twenty minutes after Mass when you receive, making thanksgiving; do not rush out of church or begin idle talk or immediately resume reading—this is disrespectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: What the Mass is (definition and sacrificial nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mass is the unbloody sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ; it is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross though the manner differs (no real shedding of blood at Mass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mass is also a Sacrament because it has (1) the outward sign (appearance of bread and wine), (2) the inward grace (Jesus Christ Himself), and (3) institution by Our Lord. The ends of the sacrifice are to honor and glorify God, to thank Him, to satisfy divine justice for sins, and to obtain graces.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the Mass is offered and the consecration
rubrics_metrics.description: The bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ at the consecration in the Mass, effected by Jesus Christ through the ministry of His priests using the words of consecration ('This is My body; this is My blood').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consecration occurs during the Canon of the Mass just before the Elevation. The offertory precedes the Canon: the priest offers up the bread and wine, and the Canon (unchanging part of Mass) runs from the Sanctus to the time the chalice is again covered. The Elevation follows consecration, with the bell to call attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priest's role, persona Christi, and the symbolism of vestments
rubrics_metrics.description: At the altar the priest is there in the place of Our Lord Himself; it is Our Lord who offers up the sacrifice, and the priest is His instrument. The priest wears vestments (amice, alb, cincture, maniple, stole, chasuble) which have symbolic meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vestment colors and meanings: white (innocence; feasts of Our Lord, Blessed Virgin, some saints), red (love; feasts of the Holy Ghost and martyrs), green (hope; Ordinary Time), violet (penance; Advent and Lent), black (sorrow; Good Friday and Masses for the dead). Symbols: amice=preparation against the devil; alb=symbol of innocence; cincture=charity; maniple=penance; stole=immortality; chasuble=love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation of the Blessed Sacrament and Benediction
rubrics_metrics.description: After consecration the priest may reserve consecrated small Hosts in the tabernacle; for Benediction a consecrated host placed in a monstrance is used to bless the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The monstrance is made to represent rays of light coming from the Blessed Sacrament. Benediction is viewed as a special blessing from Our Lord Himself; the faithful are encouraged to attend and show reverence rather than indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting at Mass: reverent demeanor and interior recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: We should assist at Mass with great interior recollection and piety and with every outward mark of respect and devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show indifference (talking, looking around) or disrespect; keep eyes fixed on the presence of Our Lord; behave as if in the presence of a king—bowing, kneeling, and showing humility. Indifference or absence is displeasing and sinful.
